theme: Hagar and Ishmael; circumcision as covenant sign
readingInstruction: Read Genesis 16:1-17:27 carefully. These two chapters belong together: Genesis 16 shows Abram and Sarai trying to fulfill God’s promise their own way through Hagar, and Genesis 17 shows God responding with renewed promise and the institution of circumcision as the sign of the covenant.
settingTheScene: It has been more than ten years since the promise. Abram is 86. Sarai is 76 and still childless. Faith and waiting wear on a person. Today’s reading shows what happens when waiting becomes too painful, and what God does when his people take matters into their own hands. Genesis 16 is the Hagar story. Genesis 17 is God’s reset: a renewed covenant, new names for Abram and Sarai, and the sign of circumcision marking every male in the household as belonging to the covenant.
observation: Sarai’s proposal, that Abram conceive a child through Hagar, was a culturally accepted practice in the ancient Near East, but it was outside God’s promise.
Hagar conceives, and immediately the relationship sours. Hagar despises Sarai; Sarai blames Abram; Abram passes the buck back to Sarai.
God meets Hagar in the wilderness, the first appearance of “the angel of the LORD” in Scripture. He sees her and names her son Ishmael (“God hears”).
Hagar names God: “You are a God of seeing.” She is the only person in the Bible to give God a name.
Thirteen years pass between chapter 16 and chapter 17, silence between them.
God appears as “God Almighty” (El Shaddai), a name that emphasizes power adequate to the impossible.
Abram’s name is changed to Abraham (“father of many”). Sarai becomes Sarah. Names matter; identity is being reshaped.
Circumcision is instituted as the sign of the covenant, applied to every male in the household, including servants and the not-yet-born Isaac.
God repeats and intensifies the promise: nations will come from Abraham; kings will descend from him; the land is given as an everlasting possession.
When God promises Isaac will be born to Sarah, Abraham laughs. God names the coming son Isaac, which means “he laughs.”
interpretation:
Genesis 16 and 17 belong together as a pair. They show what faith and unbelief look like when waiting on God’s promise. Genesis 16 is unbelief masquerading as practical wisdom. Genesis 17 is faith renewed by God himself.

The Hagar episode is a study in what happens when believers try to help God fulfill his promises through ungodly means. Sarai’s proposal was culturally normal in the ancient Near East. A barren wife could have a child through her servant, and the child would legally be considered hers. From a human standpoint, it was a reasonable plan. From God’s standpoint, it was a substitute. God had promised a child through Sarai. The child Sarai wanted through Hagar was not the promised child.

The consequences come quickly. Hagar conceives and despises her mistress. Sarai blames Abram for the situation she created. Abram refuses to lead and passes the problem back to Sarai. The household fractures. Hagar flees into the wilderness. This is what happens when believers try to manufacture God’s promises through their own ingenuity. The results are bitterness, blame, and broken relationships. God’s promises cannot be helped along by human strategy. They can only be received in faith.

But notice what God does for Hagar. He meets her in the wilderness. The angel of the LORD, almost certainly a pre-incarnate appearance of Christ, speaks to her by name. He hears her affliction. He gives her a promise about her son. Hagar’s response is one of the most remarkable confessions in the Bible: “You are a God of seeing… Truly here I have seen him who looks after me.” Hagar is the only person in Scripture who gives God a name. And the God she names is the God who sees the rejected, the abandoned, the wronged. This is who God is. Even in the middle of human failure, he meets the casualties with personal kindness.

Thirteen years of silence pass between chapters 16 and 17. Long silences are common in the patriarchal narratives. Faith must learn to wait. And then God appears again to Abram, this time as “God Almighty”, El Shaddai. The name emphasizes God’s power to do what nothing and no one else can do. It is the right name for this moment, because what God is about to promise is impossible.

The covenant is renewed with significant changes. Abram becomes Abraham, “father of a multitude.” Sarai becomes Sarah, “princess.” Names are not arbitrary in Scripture; they carry identity. By renaming them, God is reshaping who they are. They will live, from this point forward, as the people whose new identities reflect the promised future.

The sign of the covenant is introduced: circumcision. Every male in Abraham’s household, including the servants, is to be circumcised. Why this sign? Several reasons. It marks the body, a permanent, irreversible sign of belonging to the covenant. It marks the organ of procreation, the means by which the promised line will continue. And it costs something, a literal cutting of the flesh that reminds the bearer that covenant entails cost. Paul will later argue that this sign was meant to anticipate the deeper cutting of the heart that the new covenant brings (Romans 2:29).

The chapter ends with Abraham laughing. God promises that Sarah will bear a son within the year, and Abraham falls on his face laughing, a complex laughter that is part joy, part disbelief, part wonder. God responds by naming the coming child Isaac, which means “he laughs.” The first laughter in the Bible is the laughter of doubt; the next will be Sarah’s laughter when she overhears the same promise. But God transforms their doubt-laughter into the name of the promised son. The God of grace turns even the patriarchs’ unbelief into a memorial of his faithfulness.
connection: The Abrahamic Covenant was cut in Genesis 15 with God alone walking through the pieces. Here in Genesis 17, it is renewed and given a sign, circumcision. Every Israelite from this point forward will bear in his body the mark of belonging to Abraham’s covenant. The sign points forward to the deeper reality of the new covenant, where the heart itself is circumcised by the Spirit (Romans 2:29; Colossians 2:11). The Hagar episode also looks forward, Paul will use Hagar and Sarah as a contrast between the old covenant (children of slavery) and the new (children of promise) in Galatians 4.
application:
Wait. This is the lesson of these two chapters. When God makes a promise, the temptation is always to help him keep it through our own ingenuity. We propose Hagars. We construct alternatives. We persuade ourselves that we are being practical. And we wreck things in the process. Today, ask yourself: is there a promise of God that you have been trying to manufacture through worldly means? A relationship you are trying to force? An outcome you are trying to engineer? A future you are trying to secure on your own? Bring it back to God. Wait. The same God who waited until Sarah was ninety to send Isaac knows how to fulfill his promises in his time.

And take comfort from Hagar. God sees the casualties of human failure. He sees the wronged, the rejected, the abandoned. If you are one of them today, know that the God of Abraham is also the God who sees you.
prayerPrompts: Confess where you have tried to help God keep his promises by your own schemes.
Ask him to teach you to wait, and tell him what is hard about it.
Thank him that he sees and hears those who are overlooked.
